description: We analyze NASA satellite and model data to detect significant directional changes in Earth’s environmental systems. Our focus: identify what is changing, where (including opposing regional trends), how much, and whether the shifts are statistically significant then visualize the results clearly.

details:
PROJECT SUMMARY

AETHER is a web tool that answers one question: is a place on Earth really changing, or is it just noise?
You choose a NASA measurement (haze, air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, groundwater or sea surface temperature), a region and a period. The tool draws the record year by year, fits a trend line, and gives a plain-language answer: rising, falling or no clear trend. It shows how fast the change is, with its likely range, and how sure we are, using a t-test and the Mann-Kendall test.

It addresses every part of the challenge: selecting variables, visualizing change over time, and determining what is changing, where, how much, and whether it is significant. You can also test each season, try a different starting year, and find regions changing the same way.

It matters because a rising line on a chart is not proof. Students and the public need an honest way to tell real change from chance, using real NASA data from 2002 to 2025.

PROJECT DETAILS

WHAT IT DOES?

AETHER tests whether a place on Earth is really changing, or whether the change could be chance. You choose what to measure (haze, air temperature, rainfall, soil moisture, groundwater or sea surface temperature), where (nine regions or the whole world) and when (any period from 2002 to 2025, whole year or one season). The tool turns each year into one value, draws the time series with a trend line, and answers in plain words: rising, falling or no clear trend. It shows how fast (rate per 10 years with a 95% range) and how sure (p-value), using a t-test on the trend line and the Mann-Kendall test. Tabs hold the evidence: each season, a starting-year slider, similar regions, clues about causes, and every number as a CSV download.

BENEFITS
No training needed: the answer comes in words first, with a glossary. Results are checkable: every chart names its NASA product and the original NASA files are public. It is a static website with no server and no account.

INTENDED IMPACT
A rising line is not proof of change. We want students and the public to tell a real trend from noise with the tests scientists use. Example: haze over north India is rising by 0.057 per 10 years, confirmed by both tests, while monsoon rain over Pune shows no clear trend.

TOOLS
Data: NASA Giovanni area-averaged series from MODIS, MERRA-2, GPM IMERG, GLDAS and GRACE (49 series). App: HTML, CSS, JavaScript, D3, Chart.js. Data preparation: Python. Testing: pytest, Playwright, Node.js, Pyright. Hosting: GitHub Pages. We used an AI assistant for guidance and reviewing code. No AI is part of the tool.

CREATIVITY
The tool lets you attack its own answer: the starting-year slider reruns the test for every starting year. It gives four answers, not two: confirmed, borderline, likely, and no clear trend. It finds similar places by comparing the trends of all six measurements. We measured its false alarms on thousands of trend-free series and kept them below 5%.

WHAT WE CONSIDERED?
Seasons can hide trends, so we test yearly or seasonal averages. Years resemble each other, so both tests are made stricter. Missing months are never filled in. We state the limits: short periods are less reliable, and a trend is not a forecast.

Website: https://mridulkhanna03-web.github.io/earth-trend-detective/
GIT: https://github.com/mridulkhanna03-web/earth-trend-detective
